title: RAW UNREVIEWED: Vitruvius covered-jar metal branches share a process but only white lead has a stated oven continuation
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED_NO_MEANING_CLAIM. Complete cached Vitruvius VII.12 describes vinegar/shavings/lidded jars in which lead becomes white lead after a definite interval; copper treated in the same way gives verdigris. Its next paragraph heats white lead in an oven to produce artificial sandarach. A shared process does not erase the metal-dependent products, and the later continuation is explicitly borne by white lead, not the copper product.

design.mechanism: Same-way process inheritance is conditioned by distinct metal inputs and product identities; a subsequent heated transformation consumes only the explicitly named white-lead product. Lids have an explicitly stated preventive purpose and opening exposes the result after an unspecified definite time.
design.unit: Complete cached English Vitruvius VII chapterXII paragraphs1–2, WHITE LEAD, VERDIGRIS, AND ARTIFICIAL SANDARACH.
design.contrast: Lead -> white lead -> heated artificial sandarach versus copper -> verdigris under the shared jar treatment; the text does not supply a verdigris-to-sandarach branch. Compare this staged product continuation with a generic same-material state change that incorrectly lets both outputs inherit the heating step.
design.prediction: A future frozen whole account invoking this duty must preserve branch-specific metal inputs, the shared jar process relation, distinct products, and explicit white-lead input to the oven continuation. Covering must be attached to prevention of evaporation and reopening after the interval, not recast as mere storage. No strict numerical interval, batch identity between paragraphs, quantitative conservation or impossibility of any other copper treatment is claimed.

source_evidence.quote:
CHAPTER XII
WHITE LEAD, VERDIGRIS, AND ARTIFICIAL SANDARACH
1. It is now in place to describe the preparation of white lead and of
verdigris, which with us is called "aeruca." In Rhodes they put shavings
in jars, pour vinegar over them, and lay pieces of lead on the shavings;
then they cover the jars with lids to prevent evaporation. After a
definite time they open them, and find that the pieces of lead have
become white lead. In the same way they put in plates of copper and make
verdigris, which is called "aeruca."
2. White lead on being heated in an oven changes its colour on the fire,
and becomes sandarach. This was discovered as the result of an
accidental fire. It is much more serviceable than the natural sandarach
dug up in mines.

assumptions_and_limits: Cached English historical-source translation, not diplomatic ancient or medieval Latin and not a Voynich source identification.
Same-way copper clause inherits the source process but does not claim an identical batch, vessel or lead/copper mixture.
A definite time is written without a numerical duration; no exact waiting period invented.
White lead names the second paragraph input; generic process-stage continuity is supported, actual same-batch coidentity is not explicit.
The source does not specify a copper-product heating branch; this absence is not a chemical impossibility claim.
The reported accidental-fire discovery and superiority comparison are source assertions; neither is a modern safety or efficacy conclusion.
